qa.name: Adductor Longus
qa.origin: Body of pubis just below the pubic crest and pubic symphysis
qa.insertion: Middle third of linea aspera of the femur
qa.innervation: Obturator nerve, anterior division (L2, L3, L4); most anterior adductor
qa.function: Adducts and flexes the hip; assists medial rotation
qa.opposing_muscle: Gluteus medius and minimus (abduction); gluteus maximus (extension)
qa.blood_supply: Medial circumflex femoral artery; obturator artery; profunda femoris artery
qa.clinical_note: Adductor Longus is the most anterior adductor and forms the medial boundary of the femoral triangle. It is the most commonly strained adductor — groin strain typically involves the proximal musculotendinous junction, common in football, hockey, and horse riding. The medial compartment adductors (Longus, Brevis, Magnus, Gracilis, and Obturator Externus) are all innervated primarily by the obturator nerve (L2–L4). The adductor canal (Hunter's canal) runs deep to sartorius between vastus medialis and adductor longus/magnus.

qa.name: Adductor Brevis
qa.origin: Body and inferior ramus of pubis
qa.insertion: Posterior surface of femur — pectineal line and proximal part of linea aspera
qa.innervation: Obturator nerve, anterior division (L2, L3, L4); deep to adductor longus
qa.function: Adducts and flexes the hip; assists medial rotation
qa.blood_supply: Medial circumflex femoral artery; obturator artery
qa.clinical_note: Adductor Brevis lies deep to pectineus and adductor longus — the three adductors (Longus, Brevis, Magnus) are arranged in three layers from anterior to posterior. Adductor Brevis divides the obturator nerve into its anterior and posterior divisions as they descend into the thigh. The anterior division passes anterior to brevis; the posterior division passes posterior. This relationship is a key anatomical landmark for obturator nerve blocks used in hip and knee surgery.

qa.name: Adductor Magnus
qa.origin: Adductor part: inferior pubic ramus and ischial ramus. Hamstring part: ischial tuberosity
qa.insertion: Adductor part: medial lip of linea aspera and medial supracondylar line. Hamstring part: adductor tubercle of medial femoral condyle
qa.innervation: Adductor part: obturator nerve, posterior division (L2, L3, L4). Hamstring part: sciatic nerve — tibial division (L4)
qa.spinal_levels: L2, L3, L4 (adductor part); L4 (hamstring part)
qa.function: Adductor part: adducts and flexes the hip. Hamstring part: adducts and extends the hip. Together: the most powerful adductor
qa.blood_supply: Medial circumflex femoral artery; profunda femoris perforating branches; obturator artery
qa.clinical_note: Adductor Magnus is the largest and most powerful adductor — it has a dual innervation reflecting its dual embryological origin: the adductor part from the obturator nerve and the hamstring part from the sciatic nerve. The adductor hiatus is a gap in its tendon near the adductor tubercle through which the femoral artery and vein pass to become the popliteal artery and vein — a key vascular landmark. The adductor tubercle is palpable on the medial femoral condyle and is the insertion of the hamstring part.

qa.name: Gracilis
qa.origin: Body and inferior ramus of pubis; inferior pubic symphysis
qa.insertion: Upper medial surface of tibia (pes anserinus — with sartorius and semitendinosus)
qa.innervation: Obturator nerve, anterior division (L2, L3); two-joint adductor
qa.function: Adducts the hip; flexes and medially rotates the knee
qa.blood_supply: Medial circumflex femoral artery; obturator artery
qa.clinical_note: Gracilis is the only two-joint adductor — crossing both the hip and knee. It is a slender strap muscle running the full length of the medial thigh. Its tendon inserts at the pes anserinus alongside sartorius (anteriorly) and semitendinosus (posteriorly) — mnemonic: 'Say Grace before Tea' (Sartorius, Gracilis, Semitendinosus). Gracilis is a workhorse in reconstructive surgery — its neurovascular pedicle makes it suitable for free muscle transfer to restore function in facial reanimation, forearm reconstruction, and sphincter repair.

qa.name: Obturator Externus
qa.origin: External surface of obturator membrane and surrounding margins of the obturator foramen
qa.insertion: Trochanteric fossa of femur (posterior aspect of greater trochanter)
qa.function: Laterally rotates the hip; adducts the thigh; stabilises the femoral head in the acetabulum
qa.opposing_muscle: Gluteus medius and minimus (medial rotation); hip abductors
qa.blood_supply: Obturator artery; medial circumflex femoral artery
qa.clinical_note: Obturator Externus is included in both the medial thigh compartment (innervated by the obturator nerve) and the gluteal deep rotators group. In the medial compartment context it is the deepest adductor, lying on the external surface of the obturator membrane. It is the only deep external rotator innervated by the obturator nerve (L3–L4) rather than the sacral plexus — a high-yield distinction. Note: also covered in Gluteal — Deep Rotators.
